relations.myth: Commission, journeys, judgment, and construction of the barrier
relations.note: God grants him power and means, authorizes judgment, and promises the barrier’s destruction.

relations.myth: Construction of the barrier against Gog and Magog
relations.note: Dhul-Qarnayn constructs an iron-and-copper barrier to contain the corrupting people.

relations.myth: Construction of the barrier against Gog and Magog
relations.note: Dhul-Qarnayn constructs an iron-and-copper barrier to contain the corrupting people.
Early and medieval interpreters identify Dhul-Qarnayn with the legendary Macedonian conqueror.
Yemeni tradition identifies Dhul-Qarnayn as a Himyarite Tubbaʿ named Ṣaʿb.
Modern Muslim interpreters identify him with Cyrus through empire and two-horned symbolism.
Medieval chronological harmonizations sometimes identify Dhul-Qarnayn with the Iranian hero Afrīdūn.

relations.myth: Quest for the Water of Life
relations.note: Khidr serves as minister, guide, or vanguard commander during the immortality quest.

relations.myth: Khidr discovers and drinks the Water of Life
relations.note: Khidr gains immortality from the spring that Dhul-Qarnayn unsuccessfully seeks.

relations.myth: Angel reveals the Water of Life
relations.note: The angelic companion tells Dhul-Qarnayn about the Water of Life.
In some unstable recensions, the angel gives Dhul-Qarnayn a wondrous stone.

relations.myth: Embracing Abraham’s faith and circumambulating the Kaʿba
relations.note: Dhul-Qarnayn allegedly accepts Abraham’s faith and circumambulates the Kaʿba with him.
Ishmael appears beside Abraham and Dhul-Qarnayn in later Kaʿba traditions.

relations.myth: Coordination with the Moses and divine servant episode
relations.note: Later texts conflate or coordinate Moses’s preceding Qur’anic episode with Dhul-Qarnayn’s cycle.

relations.myth: Iskandar, Khidr, and Ilyas at the wall
relations.note: Persian traditions place Elijah beside Khidr and Iskandar during the barrier episode.
